Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.
  • Industry observers note that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024.
  • It has been revealed that as of October 2026, data center developers have unveiled intends for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence firm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

Industry observers note that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

It has been revealed that as of October 2026, data center developers have unveiled intends for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence firm. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

It has been revealed that building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a newly introduced industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

According to recent reports, rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some key questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” states Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont states.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building newly introduced fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi notes.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.).

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi notes. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of revealed projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

According to recent reports, and while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

It has been revealed that creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

In a recent development, “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp notes. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a latest looped transformer model.
  • Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • In a recent development, we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a latest looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

In a recent development, we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

Industry observers note that pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility of AI consciousness as a risk factor for investors, warning that it might introduce new rules to protect its models. But that stance came under fire from an inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel, best known for his essay about what it's like to be a bat, was blunt. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he remarked. He argued that producing language isn't enough to establish consciousness. But other philosophers disagree.

Here's why language has become central to the debate over conscious AI.

According to recent reports, AI agents in Amazon Connect Customer can now populate fields of a step-by-step guide for contact center agents during live customer interactions. With step-by-step guides, managers can design forms and other user interfaces for common workflows, such as rebooking a trip or submitting a claim. Now, AI agents can fill in a guide when it first loads and suggest updates during live conversations, saving time and improving data accuracy.

Sources indicate that when contact center agents speak to customers, they spend valuable time recording the information they need to solve the customer's problem in a step-by-step guide. For example, when a traveler calls an airline to change her flight, the agent might record her booking reference, dates of travel, and seat preferences. Now, Connect Customer's AI agents can automatically suggest and populate information like this, based on the context of the conversation. Human agents can review each suggestion, accept or reject suggestions individually or in bulk, and make any edits before submitting. The agent can focus on the customer and the problem at hand rather than on manual data entry.

You can use AI agents with step-by-step guides in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more and get started, see step-by-step guides in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

#32168. How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6128 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
  • Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
  • The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

Recent findings suggest that in the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

According to recent reports, AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software complications and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 demonstrates a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

It has been revealed that we’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Industry observers note that figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

Sources indicate that at the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis states 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

Industry observers note that with the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

We work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel indicates what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Industry observers note that claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

In a recent development, starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no upcoming work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Industry observers note that adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote fresh instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

Shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Industry observers note that figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

It has been revealed that baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to newly introduced spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also reveals the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

According to recent reports, such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

It has been revealed that public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Industry observers note that access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

According to recent reports, similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

According to recent reports, A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

For example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Sources indicate that harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

In a recent development, each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

Recent findings suggest that the SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

However, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

Balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

In a recent development, existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

According to recent reports, table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

It has been revealed that table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

In a recent development, our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

In a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

It has been revealed that benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

In a recent development, what a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a newly introduced harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

Industry observers note that that is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask new questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 indicates the setup.

Figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

According to recent reports, table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

Industry observers note that A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Industry observers note that domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Recent findings suggest that before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

It has been revealed that we ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

In a recent development, the model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Sources indicate that we built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Sources indicate that the D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

Sources indicate that the original instruction.md indicates why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

Figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the newly introduced parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:.

Recent findings suggest that the shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

It is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

Industry observers note that finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

According to recent reports, A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to upcoming spectra.

Industry observers note that harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

According to recent reports, when a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

In a recent development, inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each new model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 demonstrates the raman-lab results for each model.

Sources indicate that figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Industry observers note that figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Industry observers note that the comparison also demonstrates the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Recent findings suggest that inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

Industry observers note that reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The new work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

It has been revealed that task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no fresh work.

Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each newly introduced task.

Evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The newly introduced work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

It has been revealed that D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Sources indicate that defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

No-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

Rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

It has been revealed that terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

Industry observers note that amazon SageMaker Studio now provides a native developer experience for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, enabling data scientists to submit distributed training jobs, deploy models, and monitor workloads through a visual interface on HyperPod clusters orchestrated with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In partnership withTata Communications.

Industry observers note that enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.

Sources indicate that as AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study.

This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.

Key findings from the report include:.

Sources indicate that AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to people. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.

According to recent reports, AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.

AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

Sources indicate that network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.

It has been revealed that naaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.

Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant newly introduced investment and complicate operations.

Breaking: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark.
  • It has been revealed that deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction.
  • One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark.

It has been revealed that deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes.

One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking. Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions.

In a recent development, robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice.

It has been revealed that we introduce RoboTrack, a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces, Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M, a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.

RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos.

Sources indicate that our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks.

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results.

RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views.

It has been revealed that roboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold.

Recent findings suggest that every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data.

Sources indicate that to support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction.

According to recent reports, we evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better.

Recent findings suggest that roboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks. Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers.

Industry observers note that RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around.

A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos.

These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare.

Note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols.

Why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric, which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos.

This is where MolmoSpaces comes in—our robotic simulation environment at Ai2. We extend its existing manipulation simulations to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. In each episode, a simulated robot arm picks up an everyday object, such as a cup, a plate, or a block. Two cameras record the interaction: one on the wrist and one at the robot’s base, rendered in MuJoCo. Using the simulator’s geometry, object poses, and camera information, we calculate each point’s position and visibility in every frame without human annotation and filter out static points on the background and the robot’s fixed base.

The pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M for training. RoboTrack-15M has 3,000 videos from 300 simulated homes with 5,000 tracks per video, for 15 million tracks in total.

In a recent development, data generation pipeline of RoboTrack-15M. Objects, indoor scenes, and robot grasps are obtained from MolmoSpaces. We use the simulator’s geometry and camera information to calculate point positions and visibility.

It has been revealed that we introduce two models trained on RoboTrack-15M, RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. Each fine-tunes an existing tracker on RoboTrack-15M together with its original training data. RoboTracker builds on AllTracker, a lightweight model with 17 million parameters, and RoboTracker-Warp builds on CoWTracker, a much larger model with about 1 billion parameters.

Sources indicate that we’re releasing both model checkpoints so other researchers can inspect and build on this work. RoboTracker-Warp’s weights are for noncommercial use.

Industry observers note that adding RoboTrack-15M improves scores on robotics benchmarks. Compared with the released AllTracker and CoWTracker models, respectively, RoboTracker improves RoboTrack-Bench by 0.8 AJ (62.6 to 63.4) and RoboTracker-Warp by 2.1 AJ (63.9 to 66.0), with gains of up to 1.2 AJ averaged across the three robotics benchmarks. On general video benchmarks, both models perform on par with their base models. Overall, RoboTracker-Warp has the highest AJ of the models we evaluated on four of the five benchmarks. The exception is DAVIS, where BootsTAPNext and CoWTracker score slightly higher.

Recent findings suggest that improvements from fine-tuning on RoboTrack-15M, for AllTracker (RoboTracker) and CoWTracker (RoboTracker-Warp). The robotics average is taken over RoboTrack-Bench, RoboTAP, and RGB-Stacking.

Results on RoboTrack-Bench by video source.

In a recent development, breaking the gains down by source demonstrates where they come from. RoboTracker-Warp improves on every source by roughly 1 to 3 AJ, including the human footage from EgoVerse and Ego-Exo4D, even though RoboTrack-15M contains only robot arms. RoboTracker’s gains are smaller and come mostly from robot footage—clearest on DROID Franka and EgoVerse EVA.

RoboTrack-15M is the result of multiple iterations and experiments with our synthetic data. In fact, our first attempt didn’t bring any gain on RoboTrack-Bench. To find out why, we looked at a simple question: how far do the tracked points move compared with real manipulation videos? We plot this as a histogram for each version of our data and measure its distance from RoboTrack-Bench (figure below).

Recent findings suggest that how far points move in each version of our training data compared with RoboTrack-Bench, for third-person (top) and first-person (bottom) views. Distance is the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between the two histograms, with 0 indicating identical histograms. Kubric has one camera type, so the same clips appear in both rows. AJ is measured on the full RoboTrack-Bench.

Sources indicate that the histograms made it clear what was going wrong. Our first version picked points anywhere in the frame, including walls, floors, and furniture, so most points seen from the fixed third-person camera never moved. To address this, we next sampled points only on the robot and the objects it handles, which brought the wrist view close to real video and raised the score. Interestingly, we found that Kubric had the same mismatch in the wrist view, which likely explains why it alone isn’t enough for the varied viewpoints of robotic manipulation. Finally, we moved points from the robot’s fixed base and mounting platform onto the moving arm, which brings our third-person view in line with real video as well and raises the ablation score to 63.0 AJ, 1.5 points above the Kubric-only control.

Our wet-lab pipeline for guiding the robot with point tracks from a single demonstration.

Sources indicate that what does better point tracking mean for robotics? Many robotic systems have found point tracks useful as a compact representation of how objects move that can guide a policy directly. To see this in practice, we built a similar system for a wet-lab task: pipetting liquid from one vial to another.

Industry observers note that here, a robot arm picks up an electronic pipette, draws liquid from the first vial, dispenses it into the second, and returns the pipette to its holder. The task is challenging because the pipette tip has to line up with the vial opening within millimeters, and the robot needs to adjust to different layouts of vials in each trial.

Recent findings suggest that following RoboTap, the robot learns the task from a single demonstration, which we record by teleoperation and split into steps. At test time, the robot compares what its camera sees with the demonstration and uses RoboTracker to estimate the motion required to align with the vial. Because the following motion runs without further feedback, the task only succeeds if that estimate is accurate.

We compare three ways of estimating where the vial has moved:.

In a recent development, we ran each method on 20 layouts with the vials in different positions: 10 with a clear view and 10 with partial occlusion. Point tracking completed the full transfer in 17 of 20 trials, compared with 8 for object masks and 5 for optical flow. It succeeded in all 10 clear-view trials and 7 of 10 with occlusion, where the mask-based method succeeded only once.

It has been revealed that the other methods fail in different ways. Optical flow breaks down when the vials sit far from where they were in the demonstration, and masks can latch onto a similar-looking object or lose the vial when it’s occluded. Point tracking, on the other hand, follows the same vial object from frame to frame, so it handles both large moves and partial occlusion. These results suggest point tracking is a promising tool for precise robotic manipulation tasks.

Sources indicate that success rate of pipetting trials with each method, with and without occlusion (10 layouts each). A trial counts as a success when the robot completes the full transfer.

It has been revealed that we find the trackers still struggle with long occlusions, finding points when they reappear, and following small objects against busy backgrounds. Training on RoboTrack-15M improves performance, but these failures remain a challenge for real-world use.

It has been revealed that our simulations also focus on picking up everyday objects. They don't yet capture the precise movements involved in tasks such as pipette handling. A next step is to simulate these tasks more closely and test whether training on their trajectories improves tracking during deployment.

Recent findings suggest that roboTrack gives us a way to measure these failures and generate training data to address them. We hope the benchmarks, simulation pipeline, and released model help others build trackers that robots can rely on.

Sources indicate that amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use. With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For newly introduced clusters, select a supported Aurora MySQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora MySQL versions 3.14 and 8.4.10, running on Platform Version 4. To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing. To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console.
