When I first sat down with Ben and Asher Spector to discuss Flapping Airplanes, I felt both of these to be true at once.

Ben is a founder of Prod, which has promptly become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley. Asher, one year Benâs senior, is a former debate champion turned Stanford statistics Ph.D. The brothers have an eye for raw talent, and aged 25 and 26 respectively, they are building the âyoung personâs AGI lab.â Their co-founder Aidan Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at Neuralink for three years while in college at Georgia Tech. Ben and Asher believe that raw talent â the type of people who would previously have gone on to do Ph.D.s or join quant firms â are the key to unlocking the next phase of AI development. This stands in sharp contrast to the approach of focusing on âbrand nameâ AI talent at any price, which seems so in vogue right now.

There is something else that is countercultural about this lab too: they recognize that scale alone is not enough. Indeed, the lab is predicated on this notion. There is only one Internet, and weâve run out of it. Data is the bottleneck today to further AI scaling, not compute. Todayâs AI models are wildly inefficient, something that Dwarkesh Patel has recently hammered home in his interviews with Andrej Karpathy, Richard Sutton and others. Flapping Airplanes is dedicated to searching for a more data-efficient AI. The companyâs name is a nod to a more biological notion of machine intelligence.

One of the fundamental debates right now in AI is around scaling vs. research. The scaling paradigm argues for dedicating a huge amount of societyâs resources, as much as the economy can muster, toward scaling up todayâs LLMs, in the hopes that this will lead to AGI. The research paradigm argues that we are 2-3 research breakthroughs away from an âAGIâ intelligence, and as a result, we should dedicate resources to long-running research, especially projects that may take 5-10 years to come to fruition.

According to recent reports, while the divide between these two schools of thought is far from absolute â research breakthroughs make compute investments more efficient, and GPUs are required for net new research â they each lead to different tradeoffs. A compute-first approach would prioritize cluster scale above all else, and would heavily favor short-term wins (on the order of 1-2 years) over long-term bets (on the order of 5-10 years). A research-first approach would spread bets temporally, and should be willing to make lots of bets that have a low absolute probability of working, but that collectively expand the search space for what is possible.

Industry observers note that one concern I have had is that by starving Ph.D. programs of talent, and by reallocating a lot of this talent to scale-oriented work (as opposed to fundamental research), we could actually push out the AGI timeline. As I noted in a previous blog post, âcorporate politics tends to favor in vogue, consensus ideas over more radical, unpopular ones â the very kinds of ideas that can take years to prove worthwhile, and which scientific breakthroughs often depend on.â Flapping Airplanes is explicitly intended to provide a Ph.D.-like experience â true research independence, long-time horizons â while bridging the pay gap between academia and Massive Tech.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest learnings of the last decade in AI is the dramatic economic value of fundamental scientific progress. Since academia seems ill-suited to compete with Substantial Tech on this dimension right now, especially in AI, Flapping Airplanes is taking this into their own hands. And they are focused on precisely the problem that is likely to define the next wave of AI: building models inspired by the data efficiency of biology. With that as a north star, the company will make bets in a variety of directions to get there.

There are two coherent motives right now in AI. One is the profit motive, and this should inspire all application builders, given the tremendous opportunity ahead. As I have noted on many occasions, AI is so underpenetrated relative to the capability set available, it is likely to create a golden age for builders for many years to come. There is a large profit pool available, and we are in the very earliest stages of generating it.

The second coherent motive in AI is AGI, predicated on the belief that now that weâve unlocked a machine intelligence, we should push toward upleveling that intelligence. Economically, progress in this direction is likely to be extremely valuable. The question is how to take on this objective in an efficient way, with a reasonable probability that resources invested will translate into long-term positive results. Flapping Airplanes is a pure play in that direction.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most attractive aspects for me in partnering with Flapping Airplanes was the team. I have met nearly every candidate that has interviewed at Flapping Airplanes, and certainly every person the company has hired. This is one of the best teams Iâve ever seen assembled at the beginning of such an ambitious journey.

There are two core beliefs that make Flapping Airplanes different for top talent:.

A belief that young people have always unlocked fundamental science in the past (Einstein was 26 during his âMiracle Yearâ).

A conviction that AI research is not a mystical domain for experts, but a domain learnable by anyone that is smart and ambitious.

With just these two premises, Flapping Airplanes is at odds with a prestige-obsessed culture in the Valley right now. It is exactly this obsession with substance and with raw individual talent that made Ben so successful at Prod, and it is this âflame spottingâ ability that gives me confidence in the courageous effort that is now Flapping Airplanes.

If you are interested to join, please reach out to recruiting@flappingairplanes.com.

#32119. One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1204 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that my kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones.
  • I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate.
  • Recent findings suggest that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that my kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don’t meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you’re holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible substantial-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in “the drawer.”.

Recent findings suggest that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed, works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading, since it is not available on the Google Play Store.

Credit: Nick Indge Credit: Nick Indge.

The installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.

The first time you fire up PhoneBox, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.

Where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog—a collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets, such as RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.

According to recent reports, I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.

Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did try were simple to modify and worked on the first try.

While I didn’t have any major concerns with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows customers should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is at the moment unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.

All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was upcoming to the software.

According to recent reports, connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Customers are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow needs your device camera to open the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.

Recent findings suggest that these minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving rapidly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth noting: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.

As long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find new lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.

It has been revealed that phoneBox took a tablet that was forgotten in a junk drawer and destined for donation and gave it a upcoming lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, but I now have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers in your house, because this one is worthwhile.

Industry News: AWS WAF announces automated discovery and protection for LLM, MCP, and A2A endpoints using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (320 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Automated AI endpoint discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover language model (LLM), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent2Agent (A2A) endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.
  • In a recent development, discovery is available through the fresh API Gateway API Portal, which recognizes the AI endpoints among the APIs it discovers automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward.
  • Recent findings suggest that protection is available through the newly introduced AWS WAF AI Security managed rule group, which protects your AI endpoints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Automated AI endpoint discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover language model (LLM), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent2Agent (A2A) endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.

In a recent development, discovery is available through the fresh API Gateway API Portal, which recognizes the AI endpoints among the APIs it discovers automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. An undocumented, public-facing MCP server appears as a shadow API. For unprotected AI endpoints, customers can enable protection using WAF.

Recent findings suggest that protection is available through the newly introduced AWS WAF AI Security managed rule group, which protects your AI endpoints. AWS WAF implements protocol recognition and compliance checks to block malformed MCP and A2A messages. When you enable content inspection, the rule group calls Amazon Bedrock Guardrails InvokeGuardrailsCheck API to detect prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, harmful content in requests, and sensitive information in responses. You can use AI Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications. Additional fees apply, and Amazon Bedrock charges separately for content inspection calls.

Together, API Portal and AI Security provide you a complete solution from discovery of all AI endpoints in your AWS environment to protecting them, without having to write any custom rules.

According to recent reports, API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions. See the Amazon API Gateway FAQ for the list. AI Security is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

To get started, see the following resources:.

AWS WAF AI Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection blog post.

#32117. AWS WAF introduces simplified pricing

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (289 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

AWS WAF introduces simplified pricing

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (289 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AWS WAF now offers simplified pricing that follows what you protect instead of how you configure it.
  • Sources indicate that the fresh model makes protection costs predictable before you deploy.
  • AWS WAF's upcoming pricing is effective from Feb 1, 2027 in all AWS commercial Regions, including Cape Town, Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo, Calgary, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich, Tel Aviv, Sao Paulo, N.

In a recent development, AWS WAF now offers simplified pricing that follows what you protect instead of how you configure it. Previously, you paid separate charges for each web ACL, rule, rule group subscription, and capacity tier, making every security decision a billing calculation. Now, your bill follows three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply. This makes the cost-benefit trade-off easy to understand, and adding or changing rules no longer changes your rate. This fresh pricing goes into effect on Feb 1, 2027.

Sources indicate that the fresh model makes protection costs predictable before you deploy. Each web ACL now includes up to 2,500 WCU at no extra charge, up from 1,500, and you can add rules such as Bot Control common protections or the Anti-DDoS rule group without additional fees. You pay a resource fee for each protected resource, a base request fee for every request AWS WAF inspects, and a premium request fee only for traffic evaluated by advanced protections like Bot Control targeted protections, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security.

AWS WAF's upcoming pricing is effective from Feb 1, 2027 in all AWS commercial Regions, including Cape Town, Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo, Calgary, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich, Tel Aviv, Sao Paulo, N. Virginia, Ohio, N. California, Oregon, as well as in AWS GovCloud, China Regions, and AWS Isolated Regions.

To learn more, visit the AWS WAF pricing page and review the AWS WAF Developer Guide as well as the blog post AWS WAF pricing now follows what you protect, not how you configure it.

#32116. Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2121 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought.
  • Recent findings suggest that the chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in.
  • In a recent development, baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China’s Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that’s vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

Recent findings suggest that the chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

In a recent development, baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

Industry observers note that proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA, so they’re more likely to survive a few hundred thousand years. But like DNA, proteins contain variations that can help identify the species they came from. Four of the five teeth in the study had distinctly Homo erectus proteins in their enamel; the fifth seems to be some other hominin species, most likely a Denisovan (more on that below).

Industry observers note that the hominin teeth and the thousands of animal bone fragments had accumulated in a cement-like rock called breccia. Based on luminescence dating (a method that measures how long it’s been since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight) of the cave sediments, along with the ratios of uranium isotopes in the bones themselves, it looks like that breccia formed sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. That’s a wide range, but it’s enough to show that Homo erectus lived in what’s now southern China at least 60,000 years longer than we’ve previously realized.

Homo erectus emerged in Africa sometime before 2 million years ago, and they had reached East and Southeast Asia—including the islands of Indonesia—by around 1.7 million years ago. The most recent Homo erectus fossils anywhere else in mainland Asia date to somewhere between 420,000 and 400,000 years ago. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java, however, reveal that Homo erectus held on in the islands up until at least 177,000 to 108,000 years ago. That makes it a little surprising that nobody had found traces of Homo erectus on the mainland during that 200,000- to 300,000-year gap.

These nine teeth help fill in some of that gap, showing that Homo erectus was still around on the mainland all that time after all. On its own, that would be nontrivial, but the teeth also shed light on how these long-dead hominins lived, what the world around them looked like, and how this handful of hominins was related to the rest of their species. And it turns out we’ve been drastically underestimating Homo erectus.

Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University.

Four of the five teeth that Welker and his colleagues sequenced proteins from clearly belonged to Homo erectus. Careful measurements of the other four—things like the shape and dimensions of the crown, the roots, and the place where the outer layer of enamel meets the inner layer of dentine—suggest these also belonged to Homo erectus.

But the ninth tooth, from Baxian, has proteins that don’t match any known Homo erectus variants, and the shape also looks decidedly un-Homo–erectus-like, “strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than Homo erectus in Baxian Cave,” wrote Welker and his colleagues in their recent paper in the journal Nature.

But who were those other hominins? The enigmatic ninth tooth looks like it belonged to a Denisovan (or Homo longi, if you prefer). But Welker and his colleagues can’t be absolutely sure, because its proteins don’t exactly match any known Denisovan sequence, either (and there’s no clearly identified Denisovan lower second molar enamel-dentine junction to compare it to). But we do know that Denisovans lived in the wider region of mainland Asia at the time, based on fossils from other sites, and there’s no evidence of any other species running around at the same time.

“It therefore seems plausible that the Homo erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian Cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins,” wrote Welker and his colleagues.

Recent findings suggest that now, to clarify, Naxian and Baxian Caves weren’t (as far as anyone knows) places where hominins actually lived. The bones and teeth there seem to have been carried in by porcupines, with the result that “why do porcupines collect bones?” is now part of your faithful correspondent’s search history [EDITOR’S NOTE: my search history now includes “there are porcupines in China?”]. So the presence of this tooth doesn’t mean that Homo erectus and Denisovans were roommates. But it does mean they were living in the same general area at around the same time; based on the territorial habits of modern porcupines, the teeth probably came from within an area of less than 100 square kilometers. So there’s a nonzero chance that Homo erectus and Denisovans might have interacted in some way, although we have no way to know what that interaction might have looked like.

Not long after this, our species showed up in the area, and we know for a fact that our species interacted, ahem, very closely with Denisovans in this part of the world. Exactly when Homo sapiens arrived is still a matter of some debate, but some fossils from southern China that may be Homo sapiens date as far back as 100,000 or 120,000 years ago, before the major out-of-Africa migration. So for a brief period of time, there may have been at least two and maybe three species of hominins living in the rainforests of what’s now southern China.

Recent findings suggest that while the enamel proteins from four of the Baxian and Naxian teeth are clearly Homo erectus, they have a slightly different version of one particular protein—one amino acid swapped for another in the sequence that makes up the protein ameloblastin. This variant is clearly different from every other Asian Homo erectus fossil with proteins that researchers have sequenced. That means they’re probably part of a different genetic population (a group of hominins that live in the same area and mostly interbred among themselves).

Recent findings suggest that there are a handful of other Homo erectus fossils from elsewhere in Asia that share one amino acid substitution with these four, but the Baxian and Naxian ones have another substitution that the other four don’t have, which means that at some point, their population branched off from the others. By plotting that kind of information on what’s called a phylogenetic tree, anthropologists can begin to map out how different groups of Homo erectus are related and how they may have moved around in time and space. And what we’re learning is pretty cool.

“The phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population [at Baxian and Naxian Caves] might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans,” wrote Welker and his colleagues. That divergence happened more than 600,000 years ago. And half a millennium after that, it seems, one group of Homo erectus still living in southern Asia may have met some long-lost cousins.

Isotopes of the chemical elements carbon and oxygen in the enamel of not just the Homo erectus teeth, but teeth from several animal species like elephants (both the pygmy Stegodon and the full-size version), rhinos, apes, and relatives of modern cattle, strongly point to the area around Baxian and Naxian Caves having been a densely canopied tropical rainforest during the Middle Pleistocene.

Industry observers note that different types of plants use slightly different chemical processes to do photosynthesis, so they end up with different amounts of the isotopes carbon-12 and carbon-13; the ratios of those isotopes in the teeth of whatever ate the plants (in this case, pygmy elephants and Homo erectus, among others) can reveal the makeup of the local environment. At Baxian and Naxian Caves, those ratios point to a forest where the trees’ upper branches form a thick, closed canopy above the forest floor. Westaway and her colleagues say the signals look very similar to rainforests in the Amazon Basin today.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the ratio of two oxygen isotopes, oxygen-18 and oxygen-16, can shed light on ancient climate conditions; higher amounts of oxygen-18, like the ones in all five teeth from Baxian and Naxian Caves, tend to signal warmer, wetter climates. All of those clues together point to tropical rainforest, a challenging environment that most anthropologists had previously assumed that only Homo sapiens were clever and adaptable enough to make a living in.

Industry observers note that that idea, that we were the only hominins capable of making a go of it in tropical rainforests, was so entrenched that it has been considered a possible explanation for the lack of Homo erectus fossils in southern Asia after about 400,000 years ago. Around this time, the climate became warmer and wetter, allowing dense, closed-canopy tropical rainforests to spread.

“In southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of […] expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-Homo sapiens hominin taxa, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savanna-woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues.

Even on Java, where Homo erectus lasted until almost 100,000 years ago, those last groups seem to have lived in small patches of more open woodlands, while rainforests spread across the rest of the islands—another correlation that gives anthropologists reason to think the spread of rainforests may have had a hand in the extinction of Homo erectus.

Industry observers note that however, the evidence from Baxian and Naxian Caves suggests Homo erectus could survive in the rainforest, “even if such habitats did not represent its primary ecological niche,” as Westaway and her colleagues put it. That doesn’t mean that every group of Homo erectus was as successful at adapting to spreading rainforests—it’s safe to assume there were cultural and social differences among the groups that might have made some more adaptable than others. But it does mean that we’ve been drastically underestimating our late cousins, and we may need to rethink what we’ve assumed were the limits of their world.

Other evidence in the enamel of the Baxian and Naxian Caves teeth underscores that point, revealing that a few of these Homo erectus individuals spent their childhoods as much as 250 kilometers away from the cave where their teeth ended up. Bedrock in different places has different ratios of the isotopes strontium-87 and strontium-86; plants take up dissolved strontium through their roots, and eventually it replaces some of the calcium in the bones (or tooth enamel) of the animals that eat the plants. So the ratio of strontium isotopes in your bones can be traced to the area of bedrock where your food was grown during the final years of your life, while the ratio in your tooth enamel is a souvenir of the bedrock where your food was grown when you were around 2 to 6 years old and forming your adult teeth. (Modern food systems are going to be a massive headache for future archaeologists.).

Industry observers note that all four Homo erectus teeth that Westaway and her colleagues studied suggested that their erstwhile owners had either moved around between different areas or ate food gathered from different areas when they were very young. Some of those strontium ratios match bedrock as far away as northern Vietnam, about 250 kilometers away from Baxian and Naxian Caves, mostly through closed-canopy rainforest.

In other words, a handful of teeth offer enough fragments of a story to show us “that Homo erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments and that long-distance mobility into those environments may have been a common behavioral pattern rather than exceptional behavior by isolated individuals,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues. “Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question.”.

Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports OpenSearch version 3.9

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (259 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you can now run OpenSearch version 3.9 on Amazon OpenSearch Service.
  • Sources indicate that this release adds a new half-float vector type and a bf16 encoder, which store each vector dimension in 16 bits to reduce the memory and storage your vector indexes need.
  • OpenSearch 3.9 also adds gRPC streaming for model predictions and agent execution.

Recent findings suggest that you can now run OpenSearch version 3.9 on Amazon OpenSearch Service. OpenSearch 3.9 helps you reduce vector memory and storage, evaluate search quality with more large language model (LLM) providers, build more responsive AI agents, and control access to shared resources.

Sources indicate that this release adds a new half-float vector type and a bf16 encoder, which store each vector dimension in 16 bits to reduce the memory and storage your vector indexes need. New 2-bit and 4-bit scalar quantization lets you choose the right balance of compression and recall for each workload. Base64-encoded vector ingestion makes request payloads smaller, which speeds up bulk loading. In addition, radial search now uses a redesigned graph traversal to improve both recall and throughput. In Search Relevance Workbench, LLM-as-a-Judge now works with Amazon Bedrock and other LLM providers through ML Commons connectors. You can also retry failed documents, edit ratings, and reuse earlier judgments to reduce repeated LLM calls.

OpenSearch 3.9 also adds gRPC streaming for model predictions and agent execution. Responses come back token by token, so your agentic applications can show answers as they’re generated. Finally, the new resource sharing and access control framework allows you to share resources such as anomaly detectors and machine learning models with specific users and roles without granting broad access.

Recent findings suggest that openSearch 3.9 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Service is offered. To learn how to upgrade, see Upgrading Amazon OpenSearch Service domains in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).
  • Recent findings suggest that the list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration.
  • The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).

Recent findings suggest that the list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”.

The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

It has been revealed that fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

It has been revealed that given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the fresh year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

The budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

As part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

The key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission initiative that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test complications.

Recent findings suggest that NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain issues for key hardware components.

It has been revealed that “Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”.

Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them rapidly or reliably.

Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them quickly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Amazon API Gateway reveals API Portal, a fresh feature that discovers, governs, and documents the APIs and AI endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS organization.
  • Recent findings suggest that many organizations can't see which APIs are running, which were never registered, which are no longer maintained, and which lack protection.
  • Recent findings suggest that every discovered API starts as a shadow API until you choose to manage it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Amazon API Gateway reveals API Portal, a fresh feature that discovers, governs, and documents the APIs and AI endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS organization.

Recent findings suggest that many organizations can't see which APIs are running, which were never registered, which are no longer maintained, and which lack protection. API Portal builds a continuously updated inventory using AWS-side traffic logs and service configuration records, with nothing to install, no logs to forward, and no traffic to reroute, for a single account or your entire AWS organization.

Recent findings suggest that every discovered API starts as a shadow API until you choose to manage it. API Portal labels each API as public or private and identifies AI endpoints, including MCP servers, A2A servers, and LLM endpoints. For managed APIs, it flags those that stop receiving traffic or lose their owner and evaluates security posture against best practices such as authentication, throttling, and AWS WAF protection. With AWS WAF API Security, it also shows the security events detected per API.

You can publish any managed API in a documentation portal for internal teams or external partners, with your branding, Amazon Cognito access control, and interactive Try it pages. If you already use API Gateway Portals, your portals continue to work and are now managed from the Documentation Portals section of API Portal.

API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions; see the Amazon API Gateway FAQ and pricing pages for details.

To get started, see the following resources:.

Amazon API Gateway product page.

Introducing API and AI security on AWS blog.

AWS WAF API Security documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.
  • Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.
  • It has been revealed that in the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

It has been revealed that in the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries. Founders donât see the future, they teleport there.

According to recent reports, I think this is true in more ways than first meets the eye. To extend the analogy of a chess game (which I recently used in an essay on the AI race and which Will Manidis also articulated beautifully in his essay on âEndgame Playâ), outside observers see startups as temporally sequential, with a beginning (inception/ seed stage), middle (product-market fit/ growth stage), and end (IPO/ scale-up). However, the best founders actually live in all three of these phases simultaneously.

Sources indicate that opening: The opening phase of a startup involves the âmagicâ of transforming from a few people with an idea into a âstartup.â Silicon Valley excels at this magic, and Paul Graham is the prophet of the opening. There are many opening strategies, but the lean startup model has proven itself to be the most repeatable one. The ecosystem around manufacturer formation is crucial because foundational decisions made at this stage are difficult to change later, and so wisdom pays dividends.

Industry observers note that midgame: The midgame of a startup begins once product-market fit has been reached. Many startups fail before ever reaching this stage. Product-market fit requires deeply understanding a customerâs need, and building a solution. Once product-market fit has been reached, you need to build a firm â figure out how to hire people, manage people, and improve the product. You need to achieve some type of takeoff, forward momentum that will allow the business to grow from something tiny and irrelevant into something meaningful and notable. Board members exist to transmit inter-generational knowledge on midgame play. Since the nature of the midgame is always evolving, founders need to filter this through their own prism to arrive at truth.

In a recent development, endgame: The endgame of a startup is the infinite future â itâs never really reached. The endgame is crucial, because without a vision of the future, the present has very little value â see the recent SaaSpocalypse. Elon Musk is the prophet of the endgame, he has always focused on the hardest problems, knowing that ambitious problems attract excellent people and unleash them to do their best work.

Some startups seem uniquely engineered for the opening, some for the midgame, and some for the endgame. A hot AI company from Stanford students is engineered for the opening game â they will easily be able to recruit friends and a bike ride to Sand Hill road easily yields capital. A vertical SaaS company is engineered for the midgame â getting off the ground is hard and recruiting the early team is challenging, but once you unlock PMF, thereâs a clear path for how to scale it up. And a deep tech company is engineered for the endgame, itâs always clear from the moment of inception why that company should pass the âwho cares?â test.

Every startup has a different set of challenges depending on what parts of the game are structurally easier and harder. For example, a startup with a weak endgame story will struggle to raise funding without immense traction. A startup with a strong opening story is at risk of hubris, employees thinking the manufacturer has reached the promised land, when nothing substantial has been achieved. And the âvalley of deathâ is famous in deep tech, precisely because a strong endgame story is always preceded by a long, fatigued midgame. The #1 piece of advice I give friends who are starting companies is to be aware of these biases, and explicitly combat them.

What is so incredible about the best companies, and the best founders, is that they appear to be playing the opening, midgame and endgame simultaneously. In the best companies, it is always early days and there is a significant dream ahead (the opening vibe), even many years in. This is how Clay feels, even though the company is almost ten years old. Similarly, the best startups often have midgame characteristics at the opening â within a few months, they can show traction and improvement, creating a sense of forward momentum. For example, RunwayMLâs incredible open-source growth, years before Stable Diffusion. And finally, the best companies create a feeling of inevitability early, such that employees genuinely feel like they are moving the world forward. For example, Anduril pioneering modern defense tech.

One phrase Iâve often used to describe the best founders is, âNo matter what happens, they are going to win.â Alex Wangâs incredible journey at Scale from strength to strength was an early and illustrative example of this concept for me. The journey of Crusoe from crypto miner to AI factory builder is another great story of grit and judgement. What has crystalized for me now is seeing a superstructure that makes this possible â these founders are constantly holding the opening, midgame and endgame in their minds at the same time, and hence they are able to create a flexible, nimble culture that is always reinventing itself, and they are much quicker in adjusting their business strategy when the times are changing.

It has been revealed that my advice to founders is therefore this: No matter where you are in your journey, donât think about your business sequentially. Force yourself to play all three games at once â when planning product decisions, when making hires, when pitching investors. If you are in the midgame, you still need to care about opening style hires that could change the business. If you are in the opening, you need to think about the endgame, because thatâs what will inspire others to join you and help turn your vision into reality. And if you are in the endgame, you should still care about midgame momentum and opening creativity â thatâs how you will become absolutely massive. As you build your organization, each of these narratives should be getting stronger â you canât just focus on the one that seems immediately in front of you.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car.
  • In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that car buyers in New York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year.

Recent findings suggest that “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor noted.

In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee.

Industry observers note that we end people might not like having to open our wallets each month, but the capital markets sure do, and car companies love making the capital markets happy. Which is why there has been such a push toward connected vehicles. Remote start and predictive maintenance alerts are nice, but your regular payments to the car manufacturer—plus any data of yours it can sell—is the goal.

Recent findings suggest that some automakers have gone even further. Infamously, BMW and its heated seats. Like the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit, it’s a fact half-remembered; BMW North America never tried such a thing, just in countries like South Korea and the UK, and in 2023 BMW’s board said that subscriptions would only be for software-related features from then on.

Fresh York’s press release mentions heated seats but also calls out a number of other modern tech features: “enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.”.

But the way the actual law is written appears to leave a rather large loophole, at least to these eyes.

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

According to recent reports, A heated seat might not have “an ongoing cost,” but the maps and databases that enable “enhanced navigation” and “hands-free driving” systems definitely do, as these need to be constantly updated. A regular cadence of software updates also generates an ongoing cost to an OEM, arguably. And car companies pay for plenty of lawyers who really love to argue.

And so, while experiments like BMW’s seat heater subscription won’t be allowed in the state, the upcoming rule might still allow for plenty of ongoing fees for services like OnStar or Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro system we tested recently.

Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is.
  • That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV.
  • So, for the company’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

So, for the company’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to newly introduced heights of power and performance.

Recent findings suggest that that EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.

For Porsche’s new Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

Porsche isn’t saying how big the new roadster’s battery is in terms of charge capacity, only that its size was chosen to balance range and weight. We also don’t have an idea of rated range, charging speed, nor battery composition, but I can say the battery pack is based on an 800 V architecture like the electric Macan, so hopefully we can expect charging performance that at least matches that SUV’s 270 kW.

The fresh Boxster also shares a motor with the Macan. Porsche is not quoting any specs yet, but it puts out about 500 hp (370 kW) to the rear wheels on the Macan Turbo. You can place your bets on whether the Boxster application will result in more or less power. I would take the over, but regardless, it’s enough to sprint this electric roadster to 62 mph (100 km/h) in under 3.0 seconds, making it the quickest Boxster ever.

But it’s also the largest and heaviest. I was told the new Boxster’s curb weight will be somewhere in the ballpark of a current-generation 911, so in the region of 3,300 to 3,700 pounds (roughly 1,500 to 1,700 kg), meaning it has gained at least a few hundred pounds. That’s light for an EV but heavy for a roadster. Its wheelbase has grown accordingly.

Industry observers note that you can absolutely feel that on the road. The 718 just doesn’t have the same buzzy eagerness as the latest 718 Boxster or Cayman. But that doesn’t mean it’s less fun to drive. In fact, I think most people would say it’s much more fun. Nearly doubling the old car’s base power output will do that.

It has been revealed that this car, though, is about a lot more than acceleration. It still turns and handles incredibly well, borrowing much of its suspension, steering, and even chassis from the current-generation 911. Few would call a 911 a boring car, and the 718 is a step more aggressive even than that coupe.

That’s in part thanks to the response afforded by the electric powertrain, which isn’t saddled by the lazy throttle application caused by turbochargers and modern emission regulations. It’s sharper even than the latest 911 GTS, which required a trick electrically assisted turbocharger plus a battery and electric motor to bring the EV feel to a car driven by internal combustion.

To bring some of the charm of internal combustion to an EV, Porsche followed in the footsteps of the Hyundai Ioniq 5N by adding synthesized shifting and engine noises to the mix. Many cringe at the thought of an EV wailing unnecessarily, but having driven many battery-powered machines that make gas-powered noises, I can say with assurance that they always dial up the fun factor.

What they often lack is authenticity. Porsche sampled the sound of what its engineers determined was the sweetest-sounding 718: the 981-generation Boxster GTS. The fresh 718 Boxster replicates both that car’s 3.4 L flat-six and its seven-speed dual-clutch transmission, controlled by the paddles behind the steering wheel.

Enable the system, which Porsche calls E-Shift, then put the Boxster into launch control, and you’re in for a bit of a show: The car not only sounds like it’s bouncing off of a rev limiter, but the car itself actually shakes. It does this by pulsing the electric motor, vibrating in much the same way that the original Harley-Davidson Livewire did.

Sources indicate that lift off the brake and the Boxster blasts forward, again doing the sprint to 60 in less than 3 seconds. All the while, the pretend engine is screaming and running through its mock gears, either automatically or at your command with the paddles. In manual mode, the car will hit that artificial rev limiter and abruptly stop accelerating, so you’d better be quick to grab that next gear.

According to recent reports, this whole system is there to add a greater sense of emotion to the car, but it does serve a practical purpose. Slinging the 718 around the tight, twisty circuit at the Los Angeles Porsche Experience Center, I was better able to judge my speed through corners by listening to the pretend engine that sounded all the world like it was spinning happily behind my head.

Don’t like it? Press the blue button on the steering wheel and it all goes away, but I have a feeling most people will want it on, at least when they’re driving for fun. They will certainly want it on when cruising into their local Cars & Coffee, since you can hear the sound outside the car as well as on the inside.

Industry observers note that cruising is better in the new 718 than the older model as well. Its adaptive suspension, dialed down to Normal mode, handles concrete separation joints on the highway and bumpy roads without problem.

And it offers something extremely rare on the EV scene: true drop-top motoring. The top folds itself down in somewhere around 10 seconds, tucking itself neatly on top of that battery pack. It also offers reasonable practicality, with a frunk in the nose plus a decently wide if shallow trunk out back. Both are roughly significant enough to handle a carry-on suitcase or a couple of backpacks. That’s about it, though. There’s effectively no room behind the seats.

It has been revealed that so, from a lifestyle perspective, it’s a bit more flexible and a bit more comfortable than the previous-generation Boxster, and from a power and aggression standpoint, it’s on another planet. Still, there’s no hiding that increase in weight and wheelbase. This truly feels like a cross-breed between a Boxster and a Carrera, which will disappoint some purists, but if you had to pick a pair of parents for a new model, you could do a lot worse than those two.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that for each extension, you declare a configuration.
  • In a recent development, cluster extensions are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports managed cluster extensions for Slurm clusters. You can install, configure, revision, and remove managed features through the SageMaker AI console or API. The first two extensions cover observability and user management. Earlier, every observability or user management change for HyperPod Slurm clusters meant editing lifecycle scripts and then replacing or rerunning nodes. Now, HyperPod manages these features for you, and you keep lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs for your organization's own software.

It has been revealed that for each extension, you declare a configuration. HyperPod validates it and applies it to every node, including nodes you add later. It then reports the extension's status and the health of each node. The observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), Slurm job, and Slurm cluster metrics. It sends them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and you can add Amazon Managed Grafana dashboards. The user management extension creates users and groups with the same IDs on every node. It also controls who can sign in with SSH and use sudo on each node type, with local users, Active Directory, or both.

In a recent development, cluster extensions are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available. You pay only for the AWS resources you use. To learn more, see Cluster extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide, read the launch blog, or visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page.

Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick noted Monday.

It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.

Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.

“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick noted. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”.

Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi, as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.

In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown remarked. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”.

Sources indicate that late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those plans, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”.

However, on Tuesday, Utah decided to drop the criminal charges against Kalshi, McGavick confirmed to Ars. In a statement on X, Kalshi general counsel Yaakov Roth stated, “We are pleased that Utah has chosen to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi, while proceeding with civil litigation. Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized. We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets.”.

In a press release, Brown explained that the charges were dropped specifically due to the pause.

Industry observers note that “Kalshi said it would geofence Utah, which blocks access to its site in the state,” the press release said. “The company also committed to monitor for Utah-based IP addresses trying to reach its site. The Office then reevaluated its position and moved to dismiss the criminal case against the company and the individual defendants.”.

Brown threatened that the charges would be raised again if Kalshi tried to renew operations.

It has been revealed that “Utah does not allow gambling, and prediction markets are gambling,” Brown said. Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges. Every firm in this space should take note. If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable.”.

Discussion of the Kalshi pause in a Utah sub-Reddit found some Redditors skeptical of the state’s cases as potentially overreaching.

However, many top commenters seemed pleased with the enforcement efforts, suggesting that Utah may have bipartisan support among some residents. One commenter cheered on the attorney general’s efforts as “the one item in the Utah GOP’s agenda I can get behind,” while another agreed that “prediction markets are incredibly toxic and are manipulated against ordinary people.”.

Many complained that Kalshi ads flooded their social media feeds. Some suggested the state should focus on banning advertising of prediction markets, while potentially still allowing adults to trade on event contracts if they want to throw their “money away.”.

It has been revealed that fears of insider trading were also raised. One commenter laid out why prediction markets seem suspiciously designed to promote insider trading and other market manipulation:.

It has been revealed that “I’m pretty libertarian and hate banning things. But gambling and prediction markets are a scourge. Even the term ‘prediction market’ is a misnomer. Because ultimately when people with massive dollars get involved it creates a financial incentive for them to make fucked up things happen in the real world. Think about it, decades ago we understood that sports betting was a problem because it corrupted sports—something that ultimately is pretty meaningless. Then we got all these people betting on the stock market with puts and it created huge incentives to cause havoc with markets. Now if people are betting big money on politics and wars and everything else, it just means people with influence can make money by making improbable/unexpected things happen.”.

Industry observers note that one commenter joked, “I wonder how Kashi would have reacted if the judge in charge of their case had ‘traded’ $500,000 on the event of them losing the case. Not a problem at all, right?”.

On the same day Kalshi confirmed its temporary pause in Utah, a judge rejected a request from Fresh York Attorney General Letitia James to immediately shut down Kalshi in that state, Courthouse News reported.

New York Supreme Court Justice Melissa Crane stated she was “uncomfortable” granting the temporary restraining order so early in the case because “there does seem to be an indication that there would be market disruption that I’m concerned about.” Kalshi attorney Grant Mainland described it a little differently, claiming that a sudden halt would cause a “market emergency.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I think this is the ultimate relief in the case, which is improper for me to do without full briefing,” Crane stated. Instead of granting James’ request, she recommended that Kalshi take steps to address the state’s top concerns by considering “safeguards for users between 18 and 20,” who are under the state’s legal gambling age, Courthouse News reported.

According to Kalshi’s estimates, Fresh York’s Kalshi user base (1.5 million) is much larger than Utah’s, so the market disruption from the Utah shutdown may not have carried the same dire stakes for Kalshi or its broader user base.

It has been revealed that the CFTC has sought to intervene in that case, too, and it seems clear that Kalshi expects the questions of who can regulate prediction markets and what trading qualifies as a “bet” to reach the Supreme Court. Kalshi’s spokesperson did not respond to Ars’ questions on how the Utah pause broadly impacted users or the platform.

It has been revealed that so far, “three federal appeals courts have ruled that states can regulate prediction markets, while a fourth found they cannot,” Courthouse News reported. But despite the current balance tipping toward allowing states to regulate prediction markets, Kalshi appears confident that the Supreme Court will resolve the disparate court rulings in its favor.

In a lawsuit filed by a disgruntled Kalshi user, Kalshi argued that it would waste lower courts’ time to continue litigating these cases and that no case should be resolved until the Supreme Court weighs in.

In that case, Kalshi user Scott Bright alleged that he lost more than $300,000 on sports bets that were technically illegal in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that according to Kalshi, all of Bright’s claims rest “on the premise that state gambling laws reach KalshiEX’s federally regulated exchange—the question now before the Supreme Court. Plaintiff puts the cart before the horse; Defendants ask only that the Court let that threshold question be resolved first.”.

The court has yet to address Kalshi’s request to stay the case, but Bright has argued that Kalshi is trying to “sideline a case governed by binding Ninth Circuit precedent so that they can wait for a Supreme Court decision that may never come.”.

It has been revealed that kalshi did not respond to Ars’ request for a statement on Bright’s lawsuit. In their court filing, they argued that “a stay will let the Supreme Court address an issue that could dispose of every claim, will not meaningfully harm Plaintiff, and will spare Defendants and the Court litigation under a framework that may soon be displaced.”.

According to recent reports, AWS Sign-In now enables developers and AI agents to stay authenticated for up to 90 days without frequent sign-ins or consent prompts. With this launch, administrators can configure Sign-in duration, which controls how long an OAuth Sign-in session remains active, for individual IAM owners and roles.

According to recent reports, this capability reduces authentication interruptions for long-running workflows and provides a more secure alternative to static access keys by using short-lived, renewable credentials. Existing session duration limits remain unchanged unless administrators explicitly configure longer durations.

Sign-In Duration supports AWS CLI (aws login), AWS MCP Server, and other OAuth-enabled applications. It does not affect AWS Management Console sessions. Customers can configure the setting using the IAM console, AWS CLI, or IAM API in all AWS commercial Regions.

To learn more, see the AWS Sign-In session management User Guide, Configure Sign-In duration on Role User Guide, Condition Key User Guide.

#32100. How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (923 w)
